Stardust roadside sign, Las Vegas

The Stardust casino’s roadside sign at night: the name in bulb-filled capitals inside a cloud of lit four-point stars that rises to a point, on black sky.

Source
Library of Congress: Carol M. Highsmith, Historic Stardust sign, Las Vegas, Nevada
Creator
Paul Miller, Ad Art Company (roadside sign, per Wikipedia); the Library of Congress note credits Kermit Wayne for Young Electric Sign Company
Made
Roadside sign installed February 1968, lettering replaced 1991 (Wikipedia); the Library of Congress note says 1958. Photographed between 1980 and 2006.
Style
Googie (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Flashy, exuberant, nocturnal
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected Carol M. Highsmith’s photograph, Library of Congress LC-HS503-1563, 1750 × 1280 px (50 % IIIF size), in a scratchpad. Not stored.
Reviewed
2 October 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Highsmith’s note: built in 1958, fabricated by Young Electric Sign Company, with Kermit Wayne’s design chosen for both the facade and the roadside signs. Library of Congress.

Wikipedia gives a different account: Kermit Wayne designed the 1958 facade sign (216 feet long, 7,100 feet of neon, 11,000 bulbs); a roadside sign by Paul Miller of the Ad Art Company was installed in February 1968; its lettering was replaced with Helvetica in 1991; it was dismantled in 2007 and given to the Neon Museum. Learning from Las Vegas studied the 1968 roadside sign. Wikipedia: Stardust Resort and Casino.

Observed

  • “STARDUST” runs across the middle in heavy sans-serif capitals filled with white bulbs and edged in red.
  • Around the word, dozens of four-point stars of different sizes, filled with gold, orange, red, and white bulbs, form a broad cloud.
  • A few large stars are outlined in light-blue neon tube instead of bulbs.
  • Above the word the stars thin into a single column that rises to a point, like a rocket trail or a flame.
  • Rows of single dots of light fill the gaps; the ground is fully black night sky.
  • The letters have straight-cut terminals and a plain grotesque form; they may be the 1991 replacement lettering, not the original.

Why it belongs

The sign is closest to the style’s night version: points of warm light and one cool neon accent on black, with the star repeated until it becomes a texture.

The tower of stars turns a horizontal name panel into an upswept, pointed silhouette.

Borrow

Repeat a four-point star at several sizes as a field around a heading, on a black ground.

Outline a few of the stars in a cool color while most are warm, so a second hue punctuates the field.
